newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protesters uncowed despite police, cold.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protesters uncowed despite police, cold.

text.p: Serbia's opposition movement planned fresh demonstrations on Sunday, unbowed by bitter cold, snow and police pressure on the mass marches that have been disrupting the capital Belgrade for weeks.

Some 20,000 people took to the streets in two separate protests on Saturday, one of them tolerated by police but the other swiftly blocked, although without bloodshed that marred protests earlier in the week.

Saturday's turnout paled beside peak numbers of more than 200,000 in a daily tide of demonstrations since November 19 against election fraud by President Slobodan Milosevic's long-ruling Socialist Party (SPS).
Demonstrators' ranks were no doubt thinned by an onset of snow-blown sub-zero temperatures coupled with police pressure.

But protesters have taken heart from an OSCE fact-finding mission that confirmed their complaints of rigging in municipal elections last month and urged Milosevic to restore opposition victories in 15 of Serbia's biggest towns including Belgrade.

The opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) also staged modest rallies in five provincial towns on Saturday. They set their next rally for 3 p.m. (1400 gmt) on Sunday in Belgrade and have vowed to keep agitating until their demands are met.
In Belgrade on Saturday, 10,000 Zajedno backers marched shouting "Slobo murderer" after the funeral of an activist who died in a December 24 riot. Police did not interfere.

But police showed less patience with 10,000 students who tried to surge down a major downtown street after nightfall, swiftly diverting them into a pedestrian mall and trapping them there for an hour before they dispersed.
Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, said Predrag Starcevic, 39, was trampled to death in the December 24 violence by a crowd trying to flee a police charge.

Starcevic was the first fatality in almost six weeks of street protests which were peaceful and good-natured until Milosevic summoned 40,000 loyalists from the provinces into Belgrade that day to confront Zajedno.

Some 50 people were injured in a melee between Zajedno and SPS supporters. The government then banned street marches. Another 29 were hurt on Friday when uniformed and plainclothes police assaulted Zajedno activists, witnesses said.

Draskovic urged protesters on Saturday to shun violence but warned, "There is a line beyond which a man no longer puts up with (state) humiliation and terror. Milosevic is trying to take citizens across that line to provoke bloodshed".

Milosevic now has riot police shunting protesters off the streets, where they had snarled traffic, into pedestrian areas to hold rallies while he considers a response to rising international pressure for real democratic reform.

A delegation of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe led by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez urged Milosevic on Friday to reverse his annulment of opposition victories in the local elections.

Gonzalez's message was published by Politika, flagship of the government-dominated press, in an indication that Milosevic might be entertaining concessions to salvage Serbian-led Yugoslavia's urgent campaign for Western economic aid after the formal end of war-related international sanctions.

The findings of the special OSCE mission have yet to be formally embraced by the body. But most of its Western members, including the United States, have led international condemnation of Milosevic's refusal to admit election defeat.
He might now choose to turn over disputed towns but quickly order fresh municipal elections in an effort to keep a half century of unbroken communist or socialist rule intact.
But Zajedno could well boycott a new election without free access to the Yugoslav news media.

In Nis, Serbia's second-largest city, the local electoral commission ordered a rerun of balloting in 17 of 26 districts after the municipal court called on it to review the situation, the official news agency Tanjug reported.
Seventeen of the city's 70 council seats would be at stake in the rerun. Of the remaining seats, the SPS took 28, Zajedno 24 and a rightist party one seat, Tanjug said.
